Article Title: Meet the humanoid robot winning hearts in China after running 100m in under 10 seconds, faster than Usain Bolt’s world record
Article Text:
Image courtesy: South China Morning Post

Rivalry with Honor’s lightning

Strategic industry for China

Global participation

A Chinese humanoid robot named Tiangong Ultra has captured global attention after running 100 metres in 9.39 seconds, faster than Usain Bolt’s men’s world record of 9.58 seconds, according to a report by Reuters. Developed by the Beijing Humanoid Robot Innovation Center, Tiangong Ultra won its preliminary heat at the second edition of the World Humanoid Robot Games in Beijing, overtaking rival robot Lightning near the finish line.Lightning, built by smartphone maker Honor, finished close behind in 9.47 seconds, also faster than Bolt’s record set at the 2009 World Athletics Championships in Berlin. Earlier tests showed Lightning clocking 9.32 seconds, reaching a peak speed of 14.5 metres per second. Despite their speed, both robots lacked Bolt’s finesse — Tiangong stumbled into the sidelines, while Lightning collapsed and had to be carried away on a stretcher.Rapid progress since last yearThe results mark a dramatic leap from last year’s inaugural games, when Tiangong Ultra won the 100m in 21.50 seconds. Tiangong also made history by winning the world’s first humanoid half‑marathon in Beijing in 2025. Lightning, meanwhile, claimed this year’s half‑marathon title in 50 minutes and 26 seconds, faster than the pace of the elite men’s human world record.The 100m sprint is one of 51 events at the games, which also feature football, dancing, and industrial‑task contests. China has designated humanoid robots as a strategic emerging industry, betting that advances in AI and hardware will accelerate their adoption in manufacturing, logistics, and consumer applications. Investor enthusiasm is evident: shares of Unitree, China’s best‑known humanoid robot maker, surged more than fivefold in their Shanghai debut this week, giving the company a market value of about $50 billion.This year’s games, held at Beijing’s National Speed Skating Oval, have drawn 2,056 robots from 666 teams across 16 countries and six continents, a sharp increase from 280 teams last year.
Article Summary: Tiangong Ultra ran 100m in 9.39 seconds, faster than Usain Bolt’s world record of 9.58 seconds. It overtook rival robot Lightning, built by smartphone maker Honor, in the final. China has designated humanoid robots as a strategic emerging industry, betting that advances in AI will accelerate their adoption.

Article Title: Urban Company takes Kent RO to court over its water purifier ads; read 'disclosure update' to NSE
Article Text:
Urban company vs Kent RO System: What happened in court

Read the ‘disclosure update' to NSE here

This is in reference to a defamation and disparagement suit filed by the Company against Kent RO Systems Limited (‘Kent RO’) in the Hon’ble Delhi High Court (“Delhi HC”) on August 11, 2026. Kent RO launched a concerted advertising campaign featuring several advertisements and social media content through various influencers, premised on false and misleading claims pertaining to the 2-year filter life and 2-year service life feature offered by the Company for its Native M0, M1, M2, M1 Pro and M2 Pro water purifiers (“NATIVE”).

Kent RO’s advertisements falsely stated that the 2-year filter life and 2-year service life feature of NATIVE water purifiers, amongst other things, is a “marketing gimmick” and that using NATIVE water purifiers is “unsafe” and “risky” for consumers. Accordingly, the Company sued Kent RO before the Delhi HC, on the basis that Kent RO’s advertisements disparaged Urban Company and its NATIVE water purifiers and also defamed them.

The case was heard at length by the Hon’ble Delhi High Court on August 12, 2026.

After a very detailed hearing in the matter, Kent RO made a statement before the Delhi HC that it would pull down the offending advertisements that are subject matter of the suit, and will not run any other advertisement or promotional content making the same or any other similar claims regarding water purifiers offering a 2-year filter life/2-year no-servicing feature, that would be disparaging of Urban Company.

Kent RO has been asked to pull down the advertisements and social media content within 15 days of August 12, 2026. While the Delhi HC passed an order on the same date of hearing i.e. August 12, 2026- it was published on its website yesterday i.e. August 22, 2026. There are other pending matters between the Company and Kent RO, including a patent infringement suit filed by Kent RO (and a counterclaim filed by the Company against Kent RO’s patent) and a suit for tortious interference filed by the Company against Kent RO, which are still sub-judice. The aforesaid details will also be hosted on the Company's website viz. https://investorrelations.urbancompany.com/ This is for your information and record.

Thanking you,

For Urban Company Limited

Urban Company has sued Kent RO Systems in the Delhi High Court, alleging that the company ran misleading advertisements targeting its Native water purifiers. The case was heard on August 12, 2026, following Urban Company’s petition filed on August 11. In the filing, submitted under Regulation 30 of the SEBI (Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2015, and signed by Company Secretary and Compliance Officer Sonali Singh, Urban Company said it filed a defamation and disparagement suit against Kent RO in the Delhi High Court on August 11, 2026. According to the filing, Kent RO had run a concerted advertising campaign, featuring both direct advertisements and influencer-led social media content, built around what Urban Company describes as false and misleading claims about the two-year filter life and two-year service life features offered on its Native M0, M1, M2, M1 Pro and M2 Pro water purifiers.The filing states that Kent RO's advertisements falsely characterized the two-year filter and service life feature as a "marketing gimmick," and separately claimed that using Native water purifiers was "unsafe" and "risky" for consumers.The matter was heard at length by the Delhi High Court on August 12, 2026. According to the disclosure, following a detailed hearing, Kent RO told the court it would take down the specific advertisements at the center of the suit, and committed to not running any other advertising or promotional content making the same or similar claims about water purifiers offering a two-year filter life or two-year no-servicing feature in a manner that disparages Urban Company.The court directed Kent RO to remove the advertisements and related social media content within 15 days of the August 12 hearing.Urban Company noted a small procedural detail in its filing: while the Delhi High Court passed its order on the same day as the hearing, August 12, 2026, that order wasn't published on the court's website until the following day noted in the filing, August 22, 2026, which is why Urban Company's disclosure to the exchanges followed on August 23.
Article Summary: Urban Company has sued Kent RO Systems in the Delhi High Court, alleging that the company ran misleading advertisements targeting its Native water purifiers. The case was heard on August 12, 2026, following Urban Company’s petition filed on August 11. According to the filing, Kent RO had run a concerted advertising campaign, featuring both direct advertisements and influencer-led social media content. The filing states that Kent RO's advertisements falsely characterized the two-year filter and service life feature as a "marketing gimmick"

Article Title: As laptop fire reported in American Airlines flight; read FAA's advisory on what can lead to your laptop, smartphone or powerbank catching fire
Article Text:
FAA has size limits for lithium batteries on flights

Read FAA’s full advisory

Power Banks, cell phone battery charging cases, rechargeable and non-rechargeable lithium batteries, cell phone batteries, laptop batteries, external batteries, portable rechargers

Lithium batteries are required to undergo safety testing.

All lithium ion batteries are capable of overheating and undergoing a process called thermal runaway. Thermal runaway can occur without warning as a result of various factors, including if the battery is damaged, overheated, exposed to water, overcharged, or improperly packed. Thermal runaway can also occur on its own due to manufacturing defects.

Flight crews are trained to recognize and respond to lithium battery fires in the cabin.

Passengers should notify flight crew immediately if their lithium battery or device is overheating, expanding, smoking or burning.

Spare (uninstalled) lithium ion and lithium metal batteries, including power banks and cell phone battery charging cases, must be carried in carry-on baggage only. When a carry-on bag is checked at the gate or at planeside, all spare lithium batteries and power banks must be removed from the bag and kept with the passenger in the aircraft cabin.

The battery terminals must be protected from short circuit.

This covers spare lithium metal and spare rechargeable lithium ion batteries for personal electronics such as cameras, cell phones, laptop computers, tablets, watches, calculators, etc. This also includes external battery chargers (portable rechargers) containing a lithium ion battery. For lithium batteries that are installed in a device (laptop, cell phone, camera, etc.),

see the entry for "portable electronic devices, containing batteries".

Size limits: Lithium metal (non-rechargeable) batteries are limited to 2 grams of lithium content per battery. Lithium ion (rechargeable) batteries are limited to a rating of 100 watt hours (Wh) per battery. These limits allow for nearly all types of lithium batteries used by the average person in their electronic devices. With airline approval, passengers may also carry up to two spare larger lithium ion batteries (exceeding 101–160 Wh) or Lithium metal batteries (exceeding 2-8 grams).

This size covers the larger after-market extended-life laptop computer batteries and some larger batteries used in professional audio/visual equipment.

Quantity limits: None for most batteries — but batteries must be for use by the passenger. Batteries carried for further sale or distribution (vendor samples, etc.) are prohibited. There is a limit of two spare batteries per person for the larger lithium ion batteries described above (exceeding 101–160 Wh per battery).

Many airlines, both domestic and international, may have stricter quantity and Wh limits to include how many power banks/portable chargers each passenger is allowed to travel with, regardless of Wh capacity.

Please check with your air carrier for its specific restrictions before traveling.

Batteries must be protected from damage.

Battery terminals (usually the ends) must be protected from short circuit (i.e.,

the terminals must not come in contact with other metal). Methods include: leaving the batteries in their retail packaging, covering battery terminals with tape, using a battery case, using a battery sleeve in a camera bag, or putting them snugly in a plastic bag or protective pouch.

Damaged or recalled batteries and battery-powered devices, which are likely to create sparks or generate a dangerous evolution of heat must not be carried aboard an aircraft (e.g.,

carry-on or checked baggage) unless the damaged or recalled battery has been removed, or otherwise made safe. The airline may offer further public guidance on transporting individual recalled products.

For additional information on recalls, visit the Consumer Product Safety Commission, manufacturer, or vendor website.

Tip: Newer lithium ion batteries have the Wh rating marked on them. To calculate Wh, multiply the battery voltage by the Amp hours (Ah).

A passenger’s laptop caught fire on an American Airlines flight last week. According to a CBS report, the flight originated in Atlanta and had 133 people on board. The report cited air traffic control audio where the pilot said that the fire may have burned some passengers. “Cabin fire in the back of the airplane,” the pilot said adding “The flight attendants are trying to put it out now.” “I think we have about four to five passengers that were burned by the laptop. The laptop is contained about mid-aircraft,” the pilot continued.According to a Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) advisory, lithium batteries used in devices such as laptops and cellphones can pose risks on flights due to overheating. The aviation body has size limits for lithium batteries on flights because of those risks. “Thermal runaway can occur without warning as a result of various factors, including if the battery is damaged, overheated, exposed to water, overcharged, or improperly packed,” the FAA says in its advisory.
Article Summary: FAA has size limits for lithium batteries on flights. lithium ion batteries are capable of overheating and undergoing a process called thermal runaway. Thermal runaway can occur without warning as a result of various factors, including if the battery is damaged, overheated, exposed to water, overcharged, or improperly packed.

Article Title: Portronics launches Ruffpad series of multicolour LCD writing pads for kids, price starts at Rs 499
Article Text:
Portronics Ruffpad Teddy 8.5

Portronics Ruffpad Dino 8.5

Portronics Ruffpad PupX 10

Article Title: Netflix unveils ‘VOID’, an AI model that can change a movie plot
Article Text:
Netflix

How Netflix VOID works







Netflix has unveiled an AI model that can alter the scene. While this is nothing new, Netflix’s model not just remove objects from video, it understands what should happen next, essentially altering the causality. Most object-removal technology leaves a gap where something used to be and/ or fills it with a plausible-looking background. VOID goes a step further: after erasing an object from a scene, it calculates how the surrounding environment should realistically respond to its absence, and in the process it adjusts the behaviour of other elements in the frame accordingly.The model, called VOID, is a vision-language system designed to edit video footage with a level of contextual awareness that sets it apart from several existing tools.For example, imagine this scenario: A movie director has just wrapped up a multi-million dollar action sequence where the star drives straight into a fiery, head-on collision. The cars explode, debris scatters, and the scene is a wrap.But suddenly, there is request to change the scene: The character survives and drive off into the sunset instead. This would mean costly reshoots or millions spent on computer-generated graphics.Netflix’s VOID can alter the scene and digitally erase the collision, the second vehicle, the smoke, and the flying debris. It will then generate new, realistic footage of pristine pavement, making it look as though the main character simply drove down an empty, peaceful road.The AI’s ‘magic’ lies in its grasp of real-world physics. Let us understand this by a different example. If a video shows a person jumping into a pool and splashing water onto the deck, VOID can completely erase the person. It will then intelligently alter the water and the wet concrete, leaving behind a perfectly still, undisturbed pool as if nobody had ever jumped in.“To train the model, we generate a new paired dataset of counterfactual object removals using Kubric and HUMOTO, where removing an object requires altering downstream physical interactions. During inference, a vision-language model identifies regions of the scene affected by the removed object. These regions are then used to guide a video diffusion model that generates physically consistent counterfactual outcomes,” Netflix said.“Experiments on both synthetic and real data show that our approach better preserves consistent scene dynamics after object removal compared to prior video object removal methods,” the company added.Netflix isn’t keeping this powerful tool locked behind studio doors, and made the VOID model available to the public on the AI platform Hugging Face, allowing anyone to download and use it.While there are already several video-altering tools on the market, such as Runway, DiffuEraser, and ProPainter, the Netflix team claims VOID is vastly superior, as per The Register.
Article Summary: Netflix has unveiled an AI model that can alter the scene. While this is nothing new, Netflix’s model not just remove objects from video, it understands what should happen next, essentially altering the causality. The model, called VOID, is a vision-language system designed to edit video footage with a level of contextual awareness.

Article Title: Man uses AI to create minor girl’s obscene photo in Delhi, extorts Rs 1.2L over 2.5 years; arrested
Article Text:
A man used artificial intelligence to create a fake nude image of a minor girl (AI image used for representational purpose only)





NEW DELHI: In Dec 2023, a minor girl in southwest Delhi came in contact with a stranger on social media. The two started talking on the phone before the man gradually lured her into a trap — using AI to allegedly create a nude image of her, which he threatened to circulate on social media. He also allegedly extorted around Rs 1.2 lakh from her over a period.Over two and a half years later, the girl could finally summon up courage to walk into a police station and submit a written complaint about her ordeal, detailing how he started abusing and threatening her from Jan last year. In July 2025, when he met her in person, he threatened her with the image of her, she told cops.Buckling under pressure and giving in to his monetary demands, the girl started transferring the money to his bank account in small instalments. She used her mother’s account to make the payments. It was only later that her father noticed the transactions and came to know about her trauma.From the beginning of this month, the man allegedly started abusing and threatening her family members, including her father and uncle, on the phone. She also alleged that he threatened to attack her with acid if she did not comply with his demands.Last week, a case was registered at Mohan Garden police station under Sections 79 (word, gesture or act intended to insult the modesty of a woman), 351(2) (criminal intimidation) and 308 (extortion) of BNS, along with Section 12 of POCSO Act Now a major, the girl is pursuing her graduation at a reputed college. Her father is a businessman.Cops quickly zeroed in on her pursuer, Ajay Dubey (25), a resident of Ambedkar Nagar in Uttar Pradesh . He was previously involved in two criminal cases — one registered in Nangloi in 2020 on several charges, including criminal intimidation and culpable homicide, and another in Nihal Vihar in 2019 for trespassing and voluntarily causing hurt, police said.After registering the case, the cops began tracking Dubey. He was arrested a few days later when he came to Delhi to attend a court hearing. Police are checking whether he targeted others as well.
Article Summary: A man used artificial intelligence to create a fake nude image of a minor girl. He also allegedly extorted around Rs 1.2 lakh from her over a period. Ajay Dubey (25) was arrested a few days later when he came to Delhi to attend a court hearing.

Article Title: Fraudster uses Raigad SP’s WhatsApp display photo to dupe police staff, seeks Rs 50,000
Article Text:
A cyber fraudster impersonated Raigad SP on WhatsApp, targeting police personnel for money transfers, but the scam attempt was foiled. (AI-generated image)





NAVI MUMBAI: Raigad Cyber Police have registered a case against an unidentified fraudster who allegedly used the WhatsApp Display Picture (DP) of Raigad Superintendent of Police (SP) Anchal Dalal to deceive several police personnel into transferring money.On Thursday, the fraudster sent a message to Raigad SP's reader, PSI Siddheshwar Murkute, asking him to transfer money urgently. Murkute immediately realised that it was a modus operandi commonly used by cyber scammers, as the WhatsApp message was sent from an international number that was not saved in his mobile phone.Thereafter, PSI Murkute learnt that the same scammer had sent similar messages to several Raigad police personnel. Fortunately, no one fell prey to the fraud, as the police personnel were aware of this modus operandi used by cyber fraudsters.Subsequently, PSI Murkute registered an FIR against the unidentified accused under the relevant section of the BNS for the offence of cheating by personation.The complainant, PSI Murkute, said, "I had received the WhatsApp message from an international number and the DP was of Raigad SP Anchal Dalal.The message read, 'I am in a meeting and my mobile is switched off. Immediately transfer Rs 50,000 to my bank account.' I knew the message sender was a scammer. I deliberately replied asking for the bank account number by pretending to send the money. As I received the bank account number from the scammer, it will be useful for the cyber police team to trace the bank account holder. "PSI Murkute added, "One police officer had received a WhatsApp message from the same international number asking to transfer Rs 2,000 by impersonating SP madam and claiming that it was required for filling diesel in the car, and that her mobile battery had drained and she was unable to pay online at the fuel station."API Amol Jadhav of Raigad Cyber Police said, "The cyber scammers use VPNs (Virtual Private Networks) to mask their identity. However, the Internet Protocol (IP) address of the WhatsApp number used by the accused will be obtained to trace the location, and the accused will soon be behind bars."
Article Summary: A cyber fraudster impersonated Raigad SP on WhatsApp, targeting police personnel for money transfers. Fortunately, no one fell prey to the fraud, as the police personnel were aware of this modus operandi used by cyber fraudsters. One police officer received a WhatsApp message from the same international number asking to transfer Rs 2,000 by impersonating SP madam.

Article Title: ANPR camera system launched in Namakkal district to curb traffic violations
Article Text: NAMAKKAL: An automatic number plate recognition (ANPR) camera system was launched in Namakkal district on Monday to impose fines on traffic violators. The facility was inaugurated at the Namakkal–Salem Road corner junction by district superintendent of police Yadav Krish Ashok.The ANPR system will automatically detect violations such as using mobile phones while driving, riding w-wheelers without helmets and driving without seat belts. Fines will be issued digitally. The penalty amount and receipt will be sent directly to the violator’s registered mobile number.Speaking to reporters, S P Yadav Krish Ashok said, “Road accidents have claimed 348 lives in Namakkal district in the past eight months. Strict monitoring is essential to reduce fatalities. The ANPR camera system will help enforce discipline among motorists. Riders must wear helmets for their own safety and that of their families. Those indulging in reckless stunts will also be closely monitored and penalised.”
Article Summary: The facility was inaugurated at the Namakkal–Salem Road corner junction by district superintendent of police Yadav Krish Ashok. The ANPR system will automatically detect violations such as using mobile phones while driving, riding w-wheelers without helmets and driving without seat belts.

Article Title: Japan installed a 1.1 MW turbine beneath the Naru Strait, using predictable tidal currents to generate clean electricity for the Goto Islands
Article Text:
Image AI generated

How Japan’s 1.1 MW AR1100 tidal turbine generates electricity underwater

Image AI generated

Japan’s tidal energy project grows from a 500 kW pilot to a 1.1 MW turbine

Why predictable tidal energy could complement solar and wind in Japan

The engineering challenges of operating a tidal turbine underwater

Between Japan’s Goto Islands, the sea is doing something that is usually associated with wind farms and solar fields. Beneath the surface of the Naru Strait, a 1.1 MW turbine is drawing energy from water moving with the tides and sending electricity back towards land through a subsea cable. No blades are turning in the sky and no panels spread across the shoreline. The machine works largely out of sight, following currents whose timing can be forecast well in advance. Installed by Proteus Marine Renewables, the AR1100 grew from an earlier 500 kW trial in the same waters. Its deployment has given Japan a megawatt-scale tidal system designed to work with the regular rise and fall of the sea rather than depending on sunshine or changing winds.The project also demonstrates the potential of tidal power in narrow channels, where fast-moving water can provide a concentrated source of renewable energy. By placing the turbine underwater, the system avoids taking up large areas of land while tapping into a resource that follows a predictable natural cycle.Unlike solar and wind power, tidal energy has one major advantage: its timing can be predicted years ahead because tides follow the gravitational pull of the Moon and Sun.That predictability could make tidal turbines useful alongside renewable sources whose output changes with weather conditions.The AR1100 is installed in the Naru Strait near Japan’s Goto Islands. Unlike a conventional wind turbine, there is no tower standing above the water and no set of panels covering land. The generating equipment works underwater, where tidal currents pass through its three-bladed rotor and turn the machinery inside the nacelle. Electricity then travels towards shore through a subsea connection. According to Proteus Marine Renewables, the turbine was deployed in February 2025, while later company information recorded that it received Japanese certification and began exporting electricity to the grid in June 2025.The arrangement is fairly straightforward in principle, although operating it beneath the sea is not. The rotor extracts energy from moving water, the drivetrain passes that mechanical power to a permanent-magnet generator, and the resulting electricity is carried to an onshore station. A yaw system turns the nacelle as the tidal flow reverses, while independently controlled blades can alter their pitch to regulate how the turbine responds to changing conditions. AR1100 is a horizontal-axis turbine mounted on a gravity-based support structure. The earlier project in the same strait provided the starting point for the larger machine.Offshore Energy reported that the earlier 500 kW AR500 pilot operated in the Naru Strait with 97% availability in 2021. That earlier machine had a rated capacity of 500 kW and recorded 97% availability during its operation, according to the material released about the project. The experience allowed engineers to see how the technology behaved in the actual marine environment rather than only in controlled testing.The next version increased the rated capacity to 1.1 MW and introduced changes to the turbine's control systems. An equipment supply and works contract with Kyuden Mirai Energy was signed in November 2022, with the Japanese project subsequently moving towards the upgraded machine. Advanced pitch and yaw systems were incorporated as part of the work. The company says those changes were intended to improve the turbine's performance and efficiency while allowing it to deal more effectively with the changing direction of the tidal flow.The most distinctive feature of tidal power is not simply that the turbines sit underwater. It is the predictability of the resource. Solar output changes with daylight and weather conditions. Wind can strengthen, weaken or stop altogether. ClickPetroleogas noted that tidal production can be estimated in advance because the cycles follow predictable natural patterns, unlike renewable generation that is more affected by weather conditions. The electricity produced at any particular moment still depends on the conditions at the site and the performance of the equipment; the underlying movement of the water is far less of a surprise.That distinction matters when renewable sources are being combined. A grid operator cannot make the sun shine or order the wind to blow, whereas the timing of tidal cycles can be incorporated into generation planning. It does not make tidal energy constant; the flow rises and falls as the tide changes, but it makes the pattern easier to anticipate. For islands such as those around the Goto group, where space and fuel logistics can present particular constraints, a submerged source can sit alongside solar, wind and other forms of generation. The Naru Strait project is intended to contribute to reducing emissions from the islands' electricity supply.Underwater generation creates its own engineering problems. Components have to survive saltwater, strong currents and long periods of exposure while remaining accessible enough for inspection and maintenance. Getting people and equipment to a submerged turbine can also require vessels, specialist crews and careful planning. The location itself has to provide sufficient water movement, suitable depth and a practical route for sending the electricity into the grid.The Naru Strait project therefore depends on more than the turbine turning. Its subsea cable links the machine to an onshore electrical station, where the generated power can be processed for distribution. Local vessels and resources were used during deployment, with Proteus' offshore team overseeing the work, while Kyuden Mirai Energy and Japan's Ministry of Environment have been involved in advancing the project.There is also a useful way to think about the long-term promise of the machine, without treating its output as something that can be guaranteed hour by hour. The tidal timetable itself is highly predictable. Engineers can calculate when stronger and weaker currents are expected well into the future, creating a generation pattern that can be plotted ahead of time. What cannot simply be printed on that chart is the turbine's actual electricity production for every future hour: maintenance, operating conditions and other technical factors still matter.That distinction is important. The Naru Strait turbine is not a giant power station, nor does the available source material establish that it will produce a fixed amount of electricity every hour for a decade. What the project demonstrates is something more specific: a megawatt-scale machine can be installed beneath a Japanese strait, connected to shore and operated using an energy source whose basic timing is known far in advance. The water will keep changing direction. The turbine is built to follow it.
Article Summary: The AR1100 is installed in the Naru Strait near Japan’s Goto Islands. Unlike a conventional wind turbine, there is no tower standing above the water. The generating equipment works underwater, where tidal currents pass through its three-bladed rotor and turn the machinery inside the nacelle. Electricity then travels towards shore through a subsea connection.

Article Title: In 1988, a retired Ohio minister received two tiny pencil sharpeners as a gift; over the next 20 years, he collected more than 3,400 and created a museum
Article Text:
World's First Pencil Sharpener Museum

How 3 pencil sharpeners became a collection of more than 3,400

Why the collection became so unusual

What happened to the collection after Johnson's death

Paul A. Johnson had just retired from the ministry in 1988 when his wife, Charlotte, gave him an unusual Christmas present: 3 tiny metal pencil sharpeners shaped like cars. The small gifts were not intended to launch a major collection, but they caught Johnson's attention and sparked a hobby that would eventually consume much of his retirement. He began searching for unusual sharpeners wherever he travelled, building a collection that grew steadily over the following decades. Flea markets, antique shops and other places became sources for new additions, and the growing display eventually outgrew the family's home. Johnson ultimately amassed more than 3,400 pencil sharpeners before his death in 2010. The collection became known as one of the largest of its kind in the United States and eventually found a permanent public home in Ohio, where thousands of the tiny objects can still be seen today.The collection began with those 3 metal car-shaped sharpeners, but Johnson soon became interested in finding examples with unusual shapes, materials and designs. According to Ohio Magazine, his collecting eventually took him to flea markets and other places where he could search for new pieces. As the number of sharpeners grew, Johnson needed more space to display them. The collection was eventually housed in a building on his property, where visitors could see the remarkable variety he had accumulated.Johnson's collection was not simply a pile of similar stationery items. It included sharpeners made from different materials and designed in an extraordinary range of forms, turning an everyday schoolroom object into something closer to miniature sculpture. The collection eventually became large enough to attract visitors, transforming what had started as a personal hobby into a curiosity that other people wanted to see.Johnson focused on manual pencil sharpeners rather than electric or battery-powered models and sought distinctive pieces rather than simply accumulating identical examples. The sharpeners represent a surprisingly broad range of subjects. Among the collection are miniature representations of animals, buildings, vehicles, landmarks and other recognisable objects, showing how manufacturers turned a basic tool into a novelty item.Johnson also organised the sharpeners into themed displays. That arrangement gave the collection a visual quality beyond its sheer size, allowing visitors to notice how differently the same basic object could be designed. Some of the pieces are particularly old, while others reflect more recent manufacturing styles. Together, they provide a quirky look at changing design trends and the enduring appeal of novelty stationery.Johnson died in 2010, but his collection was preserved rather than dispersed. It eventually became the centrepiece of the Paul A. Johnson Pencil Sharpener Museum at the Hocking Hills Regional Welcome Centre in Logan, Ohio. The museum was later moved into a new, larger facility, reopening on January 20, 2024. The new building provides improved accessibility, climate control and museum-quality display cases, giving the collection a more permanent setting.The museum now contains roughly 5,000 pencil sharpeners, combining Johnson's original collection with additional pieces that expanded the display. What makes the museum remarkable is the unlikely chain of events behind it. Three tiny metal sharpeners given as a Christmas present in 1988 eventually inspired decades of collecting and thousands of additions, turning an ordinary stationery item into the foundation of a dedicated Ohio museum.
Article Summary: Paul A. Johnson started collecting pencil sharpeners in 1988. His wife gave him 3 car-shaped pencils as a Christmas present. His collection grew steadily over the following decades. It eventually became one of the largest of its kind in the United States. Johnson died in 2010, but his collection was preserved rather than dispersed. It is now the centrepiece of a new museum in Ohio.

Article Title: Meet Finley Holz, the Minnesota student who studied 10 years of wolf-tracking data and found deep snow can make wolves move less
Article Text:
Image AI generated

How Finley Holz used wolf-tracking and winter weather data to study wolf movement

Image AI generated

Deep snow was linked to reduced wolf movement in Minnesota

Finley Holz found wolf movement decreased as winter storms approached

Finley Holz’s wolf research earns second place in Minnesota Story Map competition

Minnesota student’s decade-long wolf research reveals effects of snow and storms

Holz combined wolf-tracking records with winter weather data, including temperature, snow depth and snowfall. Using ArcGIS Pro, he mapped wolf locations and converted them into movement data, while a Python programme helped compare movements with weather conditions. His research found that deeper snow was linked to reduced wolf movement. The study recorded a statistically significant negative correlation between snow depth and movement.However, cold snaps did not significantly affect how much the wolves moved. The research also produced an unexpected finding. Wolf movement decreased as a winter storm approached, while three days after a storm, movement was significantly below the average winter level. Holz's project was recognised in a Minnesota Story Map competition, where he placed second.Holz combined wolf-tracking information with winter weather measurements, including high and low temperatures, snow depth and snowfall events.The project used ArcGIS Pro to organise shapefiles and create maps showing wolf locations. The resulting location points were then converted into movement data. Holz also wrote a Python programme to align the wolf movements with the different winter weather conditions.The data came from wolf collar information provided by the Fond du Lac Resource Management Division. Pine Knot News, a Minnesota-based publication, reports that wildlife programme manager Michael Schrage provided wolf collar data and guidance to the students. Holz and other students also had the opportunity to collar Otter Creek wolf pups on the Fond du Lac Reservation on 5 May.One of the clearest findings from Holz's research was the relationship between snow depth and wolf movement. According to the project published in Fairfolio, titled ‘ The Effect of Winter Weather Events on Wolf (Canis lupus) Movement on the Fond du Lac Reservation’ , Holz's second hypothesis was supported: wolves moved less as snow depth increased. The study found a statistically significant negative correlation between snow depth and wolf movement. In simple terms, the data showed that as the snow became deeper, the distance wolves travelled per movement decreased.The finding in similar terms, stating that Holz "found that winter cold snaps have no effect on wolf movement" but that there was "a negative correlation between snow depth and wolf movement: the deeper the snow, the less the wolves moved." Holz had also expected extreme cold to affect wolf movement. His third hypothesis predicted that wolves would move the least during a cold snap. However, the results did not support this idea. The Fairfolio project says there was no difference in wolf movement during a cold snap compared with normal winter movement. That meant that extremely cold periods, at least within the conditions examined in the study, did not produce the reduction in movement Holz had expected.Another unexpected finding came from the relationship between wolf movement and winter storms. Holz originally hypothesised that wolves would travel the furthest immediately after a storm. Instead, the data showed that their movement declined around the time of a storm.According to the project abstract, "Three days after the storm had passed, the wolves moved significantly less than the average winter movement (p<.001)." After that period, their movement returned to the normal winter pattern. The study also found something Holz described as surprising: wolf movement decreased each day as a winter storm approached.The project says this "appears to indicate that the wolves were able to sense the oncoming storm before it arrived."Holz's wolf research also became part of a successful Minnesota Story Map competition. Two Cloquet High School students and a Hermantown student with Cloquet connections won the top three places in the competition. Hermantown freshman Gabriel Bradley came first, while Cloquet sophomores Finley Holz and Melanie Buhs placed second and third.The Minnesota Alliance for Geographic Education competition challenges students to conduct research and present their findings through an ArcGIS Online story map.Holz's project focused on the effect of winter weather events on wolf movement, while Bradley's project examined factors affecting wolf pack den relocation.Holz's project provides a detailed look at how winter conditions can influence wolf movement in northeastern Minnesota. Rather than finding that every form of severe winter weather caused wolves to travel less, the research showed a more specific pattern. Increasing snow depth was associated with reduced wolf movement, while cold snaps alone did not significantly change movement.The study also raised a new question about how wolves respond to approaching storms. The observation that movement decreased before a storm arrived suggests that further research could investigate whether wolves respond to changes in atmospheric or environmental conditions before severe weather reaches the area.For a high-school research project, Holz's work combined a decade of wildlife-tracking information with geographic mapping, weather data and computer analysis to examine the behaviour of an important northern predator.
Article Summary: Finley Holz combined wolf-tracking and winter weather data to study wolf movement in Minnesota. He found that deeper snow was linked to reduced wolf movement. Wolf movement decreased as a winter storm approached, while three days after a storm, movement was significantly below the average winter level.

Article Title: China’s 16.18-km undersea high-speed rail tunnel completes 21-day cutter replacement under extreme pressure
Article Text:
Image: AI Generated

How China’s Jintang undersea tunnel completed high-pressure shield cutter replacement

Engineers replaced 104 cutting tools under high pressure

The “Deep-Sea Space Station” allows longer work shifts

China is pushing high-speed rail through underwater environments

Deep beneath the waters off eastern China, engineers are carrying out one of the most demanding stages of construction on a high-speed railway tunnel. The Jintang undersea tunnel, part of the Ningbo-Zhoushan high-speed railway in Zhejiang Province, has completed the inspection and replacement of 104 shield cutting tools after 21 days of work under intense water and soil pressure. The 16.18-kilometre tunnel is set to become the world’s longest undersea high-speed rail tunnel, linking Ningbo with Zhoushan and cutting the journey between the two cities from as much as two hours to about 26 minutes. The latest operation also tested a domestically developed saturation hyperbaric system adapted from deep-sea diving technology. The achievement comes as China continues pushing high-speed rail construction through challenging underwater environments, including the recently completed shield-machine crossing beneath the Yangtze River, another major engineering milestone highlighted by China’s State Council Information Office . The operation demonstrates how construction methods are being adapted to underwater conditions safely too.The Jintang tunnel is the critical undersea section of the Ningbo-Zhoushan high-speed railway and stretches 16.18 kilometres, including an 11.21-kilometre shield-bored section. It will connect the port city of Ningbo with the Zhoushan islands, where journeys currently rely heavily on roads and ferries. Once the railway opens, travel between Ningbo and Zhoushan is expected to take as little as 26 minutes, compared with roughly 1.5 to 2 hours today.The tunnel is being excavated from opposite shores using two super-large-diameter shield machines. One machine, Yongzhou, must bore 4,940 metres through 24 alternating layers of soft and hard rock, representing nearly 70 per cent of its route and creating severe wear on its cutting tools. Excavation progress is being monitored carefully. The geological conditions make the project particularly demanding. Rock strength along the route reaches 191 megapascals, placing some of the material in the high-strength to very-high-strength category. As the cutting head moves through alternating rock layers, its tools experience substantial mechanical stress and wear. That made the latest replacement operation necessary, but carrying out such maintenance deep beneath the seabed presented a challenge of its own. At the tunnel’s deepest point, the excavation reaches about 92 metres below sea level, where combined water and soil pressure can reach 8.5 bar. A roughly 2,000-metre section experiences pressure above 6 bar. These conditions mean that workers cannot simply enter the cutting chamber using conventional methods and carry out maintenance as they would in a normal tunnel.The latest operation involved inspecting and replacing 104 shield cutting tools over 21 days. These tools sit at the front of the tunnel-boring machine and are responsible for breaking through the rock and soil ahead of it. Their condition is critical because worn cutters can reduce excavation efficiency and make continued tunnelling more difficult. The operation was carried out under high water pressure, turning what would ordinarily be a demanding mechanical maintenance job into a complex human-safety challenge. Global Times reported that conventional compressed-air methods provide workers with only around 40 minutes of effective working time per person each day and are generally limited to depths of approximately 60 metres. The Jintang tunnel’s deeper and higher-pressure conditions required a different approach. The construction team spent three years adapting technology derived from deep-sea saturation diving. The result was described as China’s first domestically developed saturation hyperbaric system for shield tunnelling, nicknamed the “Deep-Sea Space Station” by the project team. Rather than repeatedly exposing workers to major pressure changes, the system allows them to remain in a controlled pressurised environment for extended periods.The system consists of living, transfer and control modules designed to allow workers to operate safely under the extreme conditions surrounding the tunnel boring machine. The system can accommodate nine workers for extended periods, with crew members travelling to the work face through a transfer chamber. They can work for up to eight hours at a time, allowing round-the-clock multi-shift operations for as long as 28 days. One of the key advantages is that workers undergo a single controlled decompression after completing their assignment instead of repeatedly moving between normal atmospheric pressure and the high-pressure working environment. This reduces the risks associated with frequent pressure changes and makes prolonged underwater construction work more manageable. The technology represents an unusual overlap between offshore engineering and underground construction. Techniques developed for people working at significant depths underwater have been adapted to create a controlled environment inside a tunnel-boring operation. In practical terms, the system gives engineers more time at the cutting face while reducing the number of dangerous pressure transitions workers must endure. The successful 21-day cutter replacement operation therefore represents more than routine maintenance. It provided a real-world test of whether the new system could support prolonged work under the pressure conditions encountered by the Jintang tunnel.The Jintang project forms part of a broader expansion of high-speed rail infrastructure through some of China’s most challenging terrain. The Ningbo-Zhoushan railway is designed to bring Zhoushan more directly into the national high-speed rail network, with the undersea tunnel providing a crucial connection beneath the water separating the islands from mainland Zhejiang. The project also comes shortly after another major underwater railway milestone in China. On July 31, 2026, the State Council Information Office reported that China had completed excavation of the tunnel beneath the Yangtze River for the Shanghai-Chongqing-Chengdu high-speed railway. The project uses the large-diameter shield machine Linghang and is designed for high-speed trains travelling at up to 350 kilometres per hour without slowing for the underwater section.The two projects involve different waterways and engineering challenges, but together they demonstrate the scale of China’s efforts to extend high-speed rail through difficult underwater environments. While the Yangtze project required a record-setting shield machine to pass beneath one of the country’s largest rivers, the Jintang project is tackling prolonged excavation beneath the seabed, where high rock strength and intense pressure complicate both boring and maintenance. For the Jintang tunnel, is also another step towards completing a connection expected to dramatically shorten travel between Ningbo and Zhoushan. The Yongzhou shield machine has already advanced 3,936 metres, or nearly 80 per cent of its assigned task. If construction continues as planned, the finished tunnel will not simply provide a faster route between two cities. It will also stand as a demonstration of how large-scale rail infrastructure can be built in environments where conventional tunnelling techniques reach their limits, with workers and machines operating beneath some of the most challenging pressure conditions encountered in modern rail construction.
Article Summary: Engineers replaced 104 cutting tools under high pressure. The Jintang undersea tunnel is part of the Ningbo-Zhoushan high-speed railway in Zhejiang Province. The 16.18-kilometre tunnel is set to become the world’s longest undersea high- speed rail tunnel.

Article Title: In 2025, Mowi launched Chile’s first floating solar salmon farm; now it supplies 57% of its power and saving 36,750 gallons of diesel a year
Article Text:
Image AI generated

Why Mowi’s 2025 floating solar cage in Chile matters

Image AI generated

How battery storage keeps Mowi’s floating solar salmon farm running

Why cutting diesel use matters for Mowi’s remote salmon farm

Why Mowi’s floating solar project could become a model for remote salmon farms

For years, diesel has been a practical part of running salmon farms in remote coastal waters, where connecting to a conventional electricity grid is often difficult. That is beginning to change at one of Mowi’s sites in southern Chile. In June 2025, the company introduced what it described as Chile’s first floating solar cage at its Isla Huar salmon farm in the Los Lagos region. The installation combines solar panels fitted to the farming structure with batteries that can store electricity for use when sunlight is unavailable. A year on, the project is reported to be supplying about 57% of the site’s power requirements. It is also expected to save around 139,200 litres of diesel each year, equivalent to roughly 36,750 US gallons. The figures offer an early indication of what renewable power can do for an offshore salmon farm operating far from the grid.Mowi announced the project in June 2025, describing it as Chile’s first floating solar cage. The installation was developed with AKVA group, Alotta Energy and Fjord Maritime at the company’s Isla Huar operation. Rather than placing solar panels on land, the system puts them directly on the floating farming infrastructure, where they have to cope with wind, waves and the demands of an offshore working environment.According to the official Mowi site, the hybrid arrangement was designed to reduce fuel use and cut emissions. The company estimated an annual reduction of 350 tonnes of CO₂. Its announcement also explained how the electricity would be handled: power from the floating solar plant could either be used immediately or stored in batteries for later use. The system was initially expected to cover up to half of the centre’s energy requirements.The panels are only part of the system. Battery storage is what allows electricity generated during periods of sunshine to remain available when solar production falls. Alotta, which supplied the floating solar technology, describes the installation as a hybrid system designed to provide power continuously rather than simply producing electricity when the sun is shining.In its account of the Chilean project, Alotta said the system covers approximately 50% of the site’s energy requirements and combines solar generation with integrated battery storage. The company also operates the project under an energy-as-a-service model, meaning Mowi purchases renewable electricity rather than having to operate the entire energy installation itself. Alotta described the arrangement as a way of making the technology easier to use at remote aquaculture sites.The newer figures from AKVA group put the renewable contribution at around 57% of the farm’s energy needs. The company says the system is expected to reduce annual diesel consumption by approximately 139,200 litres. That is roughly 36,750 US gallons of fuel that would no longer need to be burned each year. The same reduction is associated with about 350 tonnes of CO₂ emissions annually.That reduction matters at a farm that operates away from a conventional electricity grid. Diesel is not only used as a fuel source; it also has to be transported to the site. Cutting consumption therefore reduces the amount of fuel that has to be delivered by boat. AKVA says the project is also expected to reduce noise from diesel generators, changing the working conditions around the farm while lowering the amount of boat traffic associated with refuelling.The project is attracting attention because remote aquaculture sites often need reliable electricity but are located far from conventional power grids. Solar panels and battery storage can provide local power, while diesel generators remain available when renewable energy is insufficient. As per Alotta, its floating solar technology was previously tested along the Norwegian coast before being introduced in Chile. Mowi developed the project with AKVA group, Alotta Energy and Fjord Maritime to improve energy efficiency and reduce emissions.For Mowi, the goal is to reduce diesel use rather than eliminate it. The reported 57% renewable contribution means solar power and batteries supply a significant share of the farm’s electricity, with diesel kept as backup. If the projected 139,200-litre annual reduction is achieved, the system could also reduce the amount of fuel that needs to be transported to the remote site.Launched in 2025 as Chile’s first floating solar-powered salmon-farming installation, the project demonstrates how renewable energy and battery storage can be added to existing offshore operations. The technology partners say the system is designed to provide about 57% of the farm’s electricity and cut diesel use by roughly 36,750 gallons a year, potentially offering a model for other remote aquaculture sites.
Article Summary: Mowi announced the project in June 2025, describing it as Chile’s first floating solar cage. The installation combines solar panels fitted to the farming structure with batteries that can store electricity for use when sunlight is unavailable. The company says the system is expected to reduce annual diesel consumption by approximately 139,200 litres. That is roughly 36,750 US gallons of fuel that would no longer need to be burned each year. Mowi estimated an annual reduction of 350 tonnes of CO₂.

Article Title: Mexico is turning corn waste and tortilla-making wastewater into building material; the strange recipe can even be 3D-printed
Article Text:
Representative Image of a futuristic Corncretl building integrating agriculture, robotics, and sustainable architecture (AI-generated image)

How tortilla-making waste became the starting point for Corncretl

Why Corncretl uses lime instead of conventional Portland cement

How robotic printing turned the corn-based material into wall panels

What Corncretl could mean for the future of construction

Every day, tortilla production creates a little-known waste stream called nejayote, the calcium-rich wastewater left behind when corn is soaked in an alkaline solution during nixtamalization. Mexican design studio Manufactura saw an opportunity in that waste, developing Corncretl, an experimental bio-based construction material that combines recycled nejayote derivatives and dried corn residues with limestone and other lime-based mineral components. The material was developed for robotic 3D printing, allowing it to be deposited layer by layer into architectural forms rather than cast using conventional concrete moulds. Manufactura says the approach could reduce carbon emissions by up to 70 per cent compared with conventional concrete, although Corncretl remains a prototype rather than a commercially established replacement for structural concrete. The project began with food waste generated by a Berlin taqueria and eventually became a collaboration spanning Mexico, Germany and Italy, showing how an everyday food byproduct can become part of an experimental circular construction system with global ambitions.The project began when chef Jorge Armando, founder of the Berlin-based catering brand Taco Kween, approached Manufactura about finding a productive use for waste generated by his taqueria. The studio, founded by designer Dinorah Schulte in 2022, subsequently developed the material during a 2025 residency at WASP in Massa Lombarda, Italy. The waste included nejayote produced during the nixtamalization of corn used to make tortillas. Rather than treating the liquid byproduct simply as something to dispose of, the team processed its derivatives and incorporated them into a mineral-based mixture. Manufactura says the resulting material combines the agricultural waste from Mexican corn processing with limestone and Carrara marble powder, linking Mexican food and construction traditions with Italian material knowledge. The collaboration also gave the project an unusual international journey: material originating from tortilla production in Berlin was transported to Italy, where it was processed and tested as a construction ingredient.One of the central ideas behind Corncretl is replacing conventional clinker-based cement with lime-based binders. Portland cement requires high-temperature processing to produce clinker, an energy-intensive step responsible for a substantial share of cement's environmental footprint. Lime-based systems can be produced using lower calcination temperatures and can harden at room temperature, potentially reducing the energy and emissions associated with the material. Manufactura says this combination allows Corncretl to reduce carbon emissions by up to 70 per cent compared with conventional concrete. That figure should be understood as a claim from the studio rather than a fully independently verified lifecycle assessment, particularly because the material is still being developed and tested.The formulation incorporates limestone aggregates, recycled nejayote and dried corn residues alongside a lime-based mineral blend containing materials such as natural hydraulic lime, silica sand, dolomitic limestone and Carrara marble powder. The result is designed to be extruded through a 3D-printing system while retaining the characteristics needed for controlled deposition.During the WASP Residency 2025 in Italy, Manufactura tested Corncretl using a WASP Concrete HD Continuous Feeding System mounted on a KUKA robotic arm. The equipment allowed the material to be extruded continuously and deposited in successive layers, demonstrating that the experimental mixture could be used in robotic additive manufacturing. The team produced prototype wall panels featuring curved, computationally designed geometries. Their internal structure was designed to help the printed walls remain self-supporting during fabrication, reducing the need for conventional external scaffolding. The forms were influenced partly by historic terrazzo patterns encountered in Italy, giving the prototypes a visual connection to the region where the material was tested. A full-scale prototype was subsequently installed at the Shamballa open-air laboratory in northern Italy, where the material could be examined beyond small laboratory samples. However, the project remains experimental, and further testing is needed before Corncretl could be considered a proven substitute for conventional structural concrete in widespread construction.Corncretl's significance goes beyond turning discarded corn byproducts into something useful. The project combines agricultural waste, lower-carbon mineral binders and robotic fabrication in a single construction system, offering a potential circular approach to materials that would otherwise enter waste streams. For Manufactura, the project also represents a connection between Mexico's long history of corn cultivation and pre-Hispanic construction knowledge and modern digital fabrication. The studio describes the material as a way of bringing agricultural residues and traditional material knowledge into a contemporary construction process.There is still a considerable distance between a promising prototype and a building material that can be deployed at scale. Mechanical performance, durability, moisture behaviour, structural reliability, environmental performance and regulatory compliance all require further testing before the material can move into mainstream construction. For now, Corncretl offers something more modest but still striking: a demonstration that the waste left behind by making one of Mexico's most familiar foods can be transformed into a printable construction material, connecting corn, architecture and robotics in a single experiment.
Article Summary: Corncretl is an experimental bio-based construction material that combines recycled nejayote and dried corn residues with limestone and other lime-based mineral components. The material was developed for robotic 3D printing, allowing it to be deposited layer by layer into architectural forms rather than cast using conventional concrete moulds. Manufactura says the approach could reduce carbon emissions by up to 70 per cent compared with conventional concrete.

Article Title: A blind Egyptian entrepreneur built an AI app that describes the world through audio, helping visually impaired users experience wildlife, objects and surrounding scenes through their phones
Article Text:
Representative image

From personal loss to a

global accessibility tool

How ScribeMe “describes” the world in real time

Pricing, platforms, and why language matters

With inputs from Reuters

When Karen Morad, a 16-year-old schoolgirl from Cairo, went on a Kenyan safari in June 2026, she experienced something she thought was impossible: “seeing” the animals around her despite being completely blind. That moment was made possible by ScribeMe, an AI-powered app created by her older brother, Mark, also blind, which turns a phone’s camera, or Meta smart glasses, into a real-time audio narrator of the world. This story, first reported by Reuters, shows how personal struggle, self-taught coding, and assistive AI can combine to give thousands of visually impaired people a new kind of independence.Mark Morad (also referred to as Mark Sedky in a report by Enterprise.com) began losing his vision in 2018 due to a rare, incurable optic nerve condition; by late 2021, both he and his sister Karen were completely blind. In school, Mark hit a wall: the screen readers he relied on would go silent when faced with charts, diagrams, and equations in physics and chemistry, leaving him dependent on others to interpret visual material. After reaching out to overseas developers with no response, he taught himself to code using YouTube tutorials and, by 2023, had a working prototype.What began as a tool to “read” academic visuals evolved into ScribeMe, an app designed especially for people who are totally blind.Recognition followed: Mark won awards in technology competitions, including the Vodafone AI Assistive Tools Hackathon in 2024, which helped bring in a co-founder and expand the app beyond document scanning. Today, ScribeMe is used by thousands of people across 140 countries and supports around 20 languages, including Arabic—a gap Mark says he found in every competing tool.ScribeMe uses AI and computer vision to analyze what a camera sees and then narrates it aloud. For users like Karen, that means hearing a running commentary on details such as what objects or animals are present, how far away they are, and what they’re doing, enough to mentally reconstruct the scene and sense the atmosphere. On her Kenya trip, Karen used the app through Meta smart glasses, which freed her hands to hold a cane while still receiving continuous audio descriptions of the safari.Beyond environmental descriptions, the app answers real-time questions through the phone’s camera and offers optical character recognition in more than 50 languages for reading documents and presentations. In daily life, Karen uses ScribeMe to find her classroom, recognize shops, choose outfits, and study more independently. The integration with Meta’s wearable glasses is particularly powerful for mobility, allowing blind users to navigate while keeping one hand available for a cane or other support.ScribeMe is available as a free download on iPhone and Android, with additional features unlocked via a fixed subscription of $20 a month or $200 a year. The annual plan effectively reduces the monthly cost to about $16.67 when paid upfront, according to reporting on the app’s pricing. Its multilingual support, around 20 languages, including Arabic, addresses a long-standing accessibility gap for non-English speakers who rely on audio descriptions to interact with digital and physical environments.For families like the Morads, the impact goes beyond features and pricing. Their father, Morad Sedky, has said that if someone had told him four years ago where his children would be today, he would have laughed it off. “Dreams grow, they grow, and we, as a family, stopped saying anything is impossible,” he added; a sentiment that now echoes across the 140 countries where ScribeMe is helping blind users “see” the world through sound.
Article Summary: ScribeMe uses AI and computer vision to analyze what a camera sees and then narrates it aloud. The app answers real-time questions through the phone’s camera and offers optical character recognition in more than 50 languages. Its multilingual support, around 20 languages, including Arabic, addresses a long- standing accessibility gap for non-English speakers.

Article Title: In 1993, a Bahamas artist began covering his home with shells, bottles, coins and tiles; decades later it became a giant dolphin-themed museum
Article Text:
PC: Bahamas Flavour UK

How Dolphin House in Bimini became a home filled with art

The Bimini history behind Dolphin House

PC: Facebook

The strong structure hidden beneath Dolphin House’s mosaics

How visitors experience Dolphin House in Bimini

For decades, one house in Alice Town, Bimini, has been slowly transformed into something that looks less like a conventional home and more like a walk-in mosaic. Artist Ashley Saunders began building Dolphin House in 1993, using discarded and salvaged objects he found around the island, at sea and at demolition sites. Shells, tiles, bottles, glass floats, coins, mirrors and pieces of marble were worked into the walls, floors and surfaces, turning everyday debris into part of the building itself. Dolphins became a recurring motif after Saunders' encounters with wild dolphins influenced his artistic work.Today, 27 dolphins feature throughout the house, helping give the unusual structure its name. What began as a personal building project gradually became a record of Saunders' life, artistic ideas and connection to Bimini, with decades of collecting and construction preserved in its colourful, intricate surfaces.Saunders did not approach the building as a conventional home that would later be decorated. The decoration became part of its construction and identity. Over many years, he collected discarded and salvaged materials from building sites, demolition work and the sea, finding uses for objects that might otherwise have been thrown away.Tiles sit beside shells. Old bottles and fishermen’s glass floats appear among fragments of marble, rusted chains, coins and cracked mirrors.Rather than being confined to a particular room or corner, the mosaics spread across the structure, covering both interior and exterior surfaces. Each surface carries evidence of his patient work, turning ordinary debris into details that give the building its distinctive character.The result is difficult to separate from the man who made it. There is no obvious boundary between architecture, sculpture and personal collection. The house became the medium through which Saunders could work with the objects he had accumulated and, at the same time, preserve pieces of the place where he had spent his life.The house is also tied closely to Saunders' interest in local history. His family has lived on Bimini for generations, with roots on the island reaching back to the period of the American Revolution. For him, collecting discarded objects was not only an artistic exercise. The materials and designs became part of a larger record of island life.That interest extends beyond the walls of the house. Saunders has written two volumes on the history of Bimini as well as four books of poetry about the islands. His tours of Alice Town combine these interests, taking visitors through the settlement while explaining parts of Bimini's past and the ideas behind his unusual home.The Dolphin House Museum therefore works on several levels at once. It is a residence shaped into an artwork, a collection of salvaged objects and a place where local history is presented through the perspective of someone whose family has longstanding ties to the island.The building's appearance can make it seem fragile, particularly where small pieces of glass, tile and shell cover large sections of wall. The underlying structure is quite different. Saunders designed the house as a substantial concrete building, with the strength needed for Bimini's exposure to hurricanes.That contrast is part of its character. The basic structure is heavy and practical, while the surfaces are crowded with colour, texture and irregular detail. A piece of shoreline debris can sit next to a carefully placed tile, while a weathered object from a demolition site becomes part of a permanent wall.Years of work turned those small additions into something much larger than their individual parts.Saunders has kept the house open to visitors, allowing people to walk through the building and see the mosaics at close range. His tours also provide context for the objects and motifs that might otherwise appear to be an assortment of unrelated decorations.The experience is closely connected to Alice Town itself. Rather than being an isolated attraction removed from the community, Dolphin House forms part of Saunders' wider walking tours of Bimini. The house offers one physical expression of his interests, while the surrounding streets provide the setting for the stories and history he has spent decades collecting.For visitors, that makes the building more than a place to photograph. Its walls are effectively a collection of references to the island, assembled gradually rather than installed according to a single architectural plan.
Article Summary: Artist Ashley Saunders began building Dolphin House in 1993. He used discarded and salvaged objects he found around the island, at sea and at demolition sites. Shells, tiles, bottles, glass floats, coins, mirrors and pieces of marble were worked into the walls.

Article Title: Canada lowered a retired Boeing 737 onto the seabed off Vancouver Island; the 100-foot jet now sits nearly 90 feet underwater as an artificial reef for marine life
Article Text:
A jet to a reef

Xihuw, is the Hul'qumi'num word for the red sea urchins that used to live in abundance in these waters

Life in a jet

Cloud sponges, plumose anemones, feather stars, octopuses, and the site's namesake red sea urchins have all colonised the aircraft's surfaces over the years.

A Boeing 737 aircraft that was originally the part of the Canadian Airlines fleet now lies nearly 90 feet underwater and serves the role of an artificial reef for marine life. The 100-foot jet was decommissioned by Air Canada due to age and structural problems, stripped of all usable components and the airframe was donated to the ARSBC. It was sunk by the ARSBC near Chemainus, BC on January 14, 2006.Now known as Xihuw, it was donated by Qwest Airparts of Memphis, Tennessee, through the efforts of Air Canada. Xihuw, is the Hul'qumi'num word for the red sea urchins that used to live in abundance in these waters but whose population has dwindled, sadly, due to pollution and over-fishing. The first step began with a phone call from Fraser MacLean of Air Canada in November 2002. The company had a Boeing 737 that was slated to be decommissioned. Fraser had seen the coverage of the HMCS Cape Breton’s sinking, and thought the ARSBC might be interested in acquiring the Boeing 737 for its second reef.The plane, which had been stripped down, weighs 15 tonnes and measures 30 metres long. The process of finding an underwater home for the aircraft proved a turbulent one, with sites considered from Vancouver to Sechelt to Courtenay/Comox and Victoria.Southern Vancouver island became the final home thanks to the community support garnered by Peter Luckham of 49th Parallel Diving.Volunteers spent hundreds of hours scrubbing the fuselage clean of grease, insulation, and any residual pollutants, ensuring nothing toxic would leach into the marine environment once it was underwater. After nearly four years of planning, including securing approval from Environment Canada and six local First Nations, the project was cleared for its final descent. On Saturday January 14, 2006, the plane was mounted on 11-foot-high support stands and lowered by crane into the waters of Georgia Strait off Chemainus.Cranes slowly lowered the decommissioned plane into the ocean off Chemainus, about 70 kilometres north of Victoria, slightly more than a month after Environment Canada gave final approval to a plan dreamed up by diving fans. The site was chosen specifically because the region lacked significant marine life at the time, having been affected by decades of forest-industry debris on the seafloor. The plane was mounted on stands about 11 feet high, positioned so divers could swim not just through the cabin, but underneath the fuselage as well. The sinking was documented for the Discovery Channel series Mega Builders.Within a few years, the ARSBC's projections of new sea life proved accurate, and today the wreck hosts more than a hundred documented species. Rockfish shelter along the wings and fuselage, lingcod rest on the surrounding sand, and schools of juvenile fish use the plane's structure for cover. Cloud sponges, plumose anemones, feather stars, octopuses, and the site's namesake red sea urchins have all colonised the aircraft's surfaces over the years.Today, the Xihwu Reef sits at a maximum depth of about 90 feet, with the fuselage itself around 70 feet down — well within recreational diving limits, though cold water and current mean a thick wetsuit or drysuit is essential. Divers can enter the cabin, now stripped of seats, and look down through openings into the old cargo holds, or make their way forward to the cockpit, where small rockfish frequently gather. A memorial plaque honouring two WWII pilots, along with a carved wooden mask that once adorned the aircraft's nose, is mounted on one of the support stands.Local dive charters regularly take visitors to the site from Chemainus, making the wreck a popular diving spot on Vancouver Island. Nearly 20 years after it was placed underwater, the 737 now serves as an artificial reef and provides a habitat for marine life.
Article Summary: Xihuw is the Hul'qumi'num word for the red sea urchins that used to live in abundance in these waters but whose population has dwindled, sadly, due to pollution and over-fishing. The 100-foot jet was decommissioned by Air Canada due to age and structural problems, stripped of all usable components and the airframe was donated to the ARSBC.

Article Title: Nominee vs legal heir: What is the difference and who has claim on assets? All you need to know
Article Text:

Who is a Nominee?



Who is a Legal Heir?

Difference between a Nominee and a Legal heir

Aspect Nominee Legal Heir Role Custodian Owner Transfer of Assets Can be done without any legal formalities. Requires testamentary documents for proof of ownership. Powers No power to transact, use, or transfer assets. Power to use and transact assets as an owner. Appointment Owner can appoint anyone, but some institutions specify certain conditions. Determined by succession/personal laws. Legal Right Cannot contest ownership legally. Can contest ownership in a court of law.

When individuals open bank accounts, invest in mutual funds, or buy insurance, they are often asked to name a nominee.However, many people mistakenly assume that the nominee automatically inherits the assets. In reality, the nominee is not always the final recipient — the ownership rights belong to the legal heir, reported ET.Understanding the distinction between these two is essential to ensure that your wealth is passed on to the intended beneficiaries.A nominee acts as a temporary custodian of the deceased person’s assets.The nominee’s role is limited to holding and managing the assets until they are legally transferred to the rightful heirs.According to ET, the nominee cannot sell, trade, or make any transactional decisions about the assets.The account or policy owner can appoint anyone — family, friends, or acquaintances — as a nominee, though financial institutions often prefer close family members.In some cases, the nominee and the legal heir can be the same person, which helps in ensuring a smoother transfer of assets.The legal heir or beneficiary is the rightful owner of the assets once the original holder passes away.To claim ownership, the legal heir must produce valid documents such as a will or other testamentary proof.If there is no will — a situation known as dying intestate — the heir is determined as per the country’s succession or personal laws, reported ET.While a nominee can initially access the assets, only the legal heir can claim them permanently or challenge ownership in court.Experts quoted by ET emphasise that having clarity on this difference helps avoid disputes and ensures that the savings reach the intended family members or beneficiaries.Therefore, it is advisable to regularly update both nominees and wills to align with one’s estate planning goals.
Article Summary: A nominee acts as a temporary custodian of the deceased person’s assets. The legal heir or beneficiary is the rightful owner of the assets once the original holder passes away. To claim ownership, the legal heir must produce valid documents such as a will.
