How Jeevan Pramaan simplifies pensioner verification



Every year, lakhs of pensioners across India must prove that they are still alive to continue receiving their pension. This verification, known as the Life Certificate or Digital Life Certificate (DLC), is a crucial and mandatory step in ensuring that pension payments are made only to eligible recipients, preventing fraud and misuse.Traditionally, this process involved visiting the bank or pension office in person, standing in long queues, and submitting a signed paper certificate. However, with the government’s focus on digitisation and technological advancement, this process has become much simpler, faster, and more convenient. Pensioners can now submit their certificates digitally from the comfort of their homes using Jeevan Pramaan, a secure, user-friendly, and Aadhaar-based platform.A Life Certificate is an official document that confirms a pensioner is alive. Without it, pension payments are automatically paused by the pension disbursing agency. This verification is essential for preventing fraudulent claims and ensuring that pensions reach the rightful beneficiaries.The Digital Life Certificate (DLC), also known as Jeevan Pramaan, is an advanced biometric-enabled version of the traditional paper certificate.Introduced by the Government of India, it uses Aadhaar-based biometric authentication using either fingerprint or iris scan to verify a pensioner’s identity. Once verified, a digital certificate is automatically generated and shared with authorised pension disbursing agencies.This online process eliminates the need for physical verification, providing elderly pensioners with a simpler and more accessible way to maintain their pension benefits.According to PIB, The submission of the Life Certificate is mandatory for all pensioners who wish to continue receiving their pension without interruption. For the year 2025, the standard submission period is betweenTo make the process more comfortable for the elderly, the government allows pensioners aged 80 years and above to begin the submission process earlier, from 1 October 2025. This extended window gives senior citizens more time and flexibility to complete the procedure without facing last-minute difficulties.The Jeevan Pramaan process involves two main steps: registering the biometric device and generating the digital certificate.Before using the service, pensioners or operators must register their biometric device such as a fingerprint or iris scanner. During registration, the user provides their Aadhaar number and mobile number, after which an OTP (One-Time Password) is sent to their mobile. After entering the OTP, they must provide their name and email ID before scanning their fingerprint or iris.Once authentication is complete, the system confirms that device registration was successful, allowing the user to move to the next step.In this step, the pensioner enters personal details such as Aadhaar number, mobile number, name, PPO number, pension type, sanctioning authority, disbursing agency, and bank account details. The system also asks whether the pensioner has remarried or is re-employed.After entering all details, the pensioner scans their fingerprint or iris using the registered biometric device. Upon successful authentication, the Digital Life Certificate is generated, and an SMS acknowledgment with the Jeevan Pramaan Certificate ID is sent to the registered mobile number.This certificate is automatically stored in the Life Certificate Repository, accessible anytime to both pensioners and pension agencies.Once the Digital Life Certificate is created, it can be electronically delivered to the concerned Pension Disbursing Agency (PDA). PDAs can log in to the Jeevan Pramaan portal to view, verify, or download the certificate directly.Pensioners can also download a PDF copy of their certificate by visiting the Jeevan Pramaan website and entering their Pramaan ID or Aadhaar number. This ensures transparency and easy access for future reference.The government provides several options to submit the Life Certificate, allowing pensioners to choose the method that suits them best.Pensioners who prefer traditional methods can visit their bank branch or a Citizen Service Centre (CSC) to submit their Life Certificate physically. Trained staff at these centres assist pensioners in verifying their details and completing the process.For those unable to travel due to age or health issues, India Post Payments Bank (IPPB) offers a doorstep banking service. Pensioners can schedule an appointment, and an IPPB representative will visit their home to complete the submission using biometric authentication. This service is available for both IPPB and non-IPPB account holders.For pensioners comfortable with technology, the Jeevan Pramaan portal provides a completely online process. By visiting https://jeevanpramaan.gov.in, pensioners can submit their Digital Life Certificate using a computer, laptop, or smartphone equipped with a fingerprint or iris scanner.The system uses the Aadhaar platform to authenticate biometric details. Once verification is successful, a Digital Life Certificate is generated and stored in a secure online repository. Pension disbursing agencies can then directly access the certificate, removing the need for physical paperwork.The UMANG (Unified Mobile Application for New-age Governance) app offers another easy option. Pensioners can download the app from the Google Play Store, search for “Jeevan Pramaan,” and select “Generate Life Certificate.”After entering the necessary details such as Aadhaar number, PPO number, and type of pension, pensioners must authenticate themselves using biometric verification. The app then generates a Digital Life Certificate (DLC), which is automatically shared with the pension disbursing authority.All pensioners who receive government, defence, or private sector pensions through authorised disbursing agencies are required to submit their Life Certificate every year. This includes:Failure to submit the certificate within the stipulated period may result in temporary suspension of pension payments until verification is completed.To ensure a smooth submission process, pensioners should keep certain details and documents ready. These include:Having these details ready helps to avoid delays or errors during authentication, whether submitting online or offline.Yes, an Aadhaar number or Virtual ID (VID) is mandatory to generate a Digital Life Certificate. The entire Jeevan Pramaan system is based on Aadhaar authentication, which ensures accuracy and prevents fraud. Pensioners must make sure their Aadhaar is linked with their mobile number and bank account before attempting to generate the certificate.The Digital Life Certificate is fully valid and legally recognised under the Information Technology Act. Pension disbursing authorities across India accept it as an official document, equivalent to the traditional paper-based life certificate.Its biometric verification system makes it secure and tamper-proof, reducing the chances of wrongful pension disbursal or misuse of pension funds.Before the introduction of Jeevan Pramaan, pensioners often faced difficulties in submitting their certificates, especially those with health problems or limited mobility. The digital system has removed these challenges, allowing pensioners to submit their verification anytime and anywhere.By integrating biometric technology and Aadhaar authentication, Jeevan Pramaan has streamlined pension management, improving efficiency for both pensioners and government departments. It also enhances transparency and ensures that genuine beneficiaries receive payments on time.
Article Summary: A Life Certificate is an official document that confirms a pensioner is alive. Without it, pension payments are automatically paused by the pension disbursing agency. This verification is essential for preventing fraudulent claims and ensuring that pensions reach the rightful beneficiaries. The Digital Life Certificate (DLC), also known as Jeevan Pramaan, is an advanced biometric- enabled version of the traditional paper certificate.

Article Title: How to get your CIBIL credit score without a PAN card
Article Text:
Your credit score is a three-digit number that reflects your creditworthiness and repayment capacity.

What is a CIBIL score?

How to get your CIBIL Credit score without a PAN Card

Factors affecting your CIBIL score

CIBIL credit score : Understanding your creditworthiness is pivotal in today's financial landscape, especially when seeking loans or credit cards. The Credit Information Bureau (India) Limited, commonly known as CIBIL, plays an important role in this regard by providing credit scores to borrowers.According to ET, credit score helps banks make informed decisions about extending credit cards and loans. Your credit history influences your CIBIL score , which is calculated using a special method.Your CIBIL score is a three-digit number that reflects your creditworthiness and repayment capacity. Ranging from 300 to 900, a higher score indicates a stronger likelihood of loan approval. Banks and financial institutions use this score to assess the risk associated with lending money.1. Go to the official CIBIL website and click on 'Personal CIBIL score,' then 'Get Your Free CIBIL score.' Follow the link provided and fill in all the required details.2. If you don’t have a PAN Card, you can use an alternative identification such as Passport, Voter ID, Driver’s License, or Ration Card. Enter the number of the chosen ID.3. Provide your date of birth, PIN code, and select your state. Finally, enter your mobile number and click on ‘Accept and Continue’.4. Authenticate your identity by entering the OTP (One-Time Password) delivered to your mobile device on the next screen. Click 'Continue' to proceed.5. Choose whether you want to link the device with your account. Select 'Yes' or 'No' based on your preference.6. Upon successful registration, you will see a page confirming that 'You have successfully registered!'7. Click on ‘Go to Dashboard’ to access and view your CIBIL score.The factors influencing the new CIBIL score, as stated on the CIBIL website, include:1. Depth of credit: This refers to the duration of your existing credit history, calculated from the opening date of your oldest credit account.2. Long-term trend of outstanding balances: The overall trend of outstanding balances over time affects your score.3. Transaction history on credit cards: How you manage transactions on your credit cards impacts your score.4. Ratio of actual repayment amount to total amount due: This ratio indicates your repayment behavior and influences your score accordingly.5. Number of new accounts opened and number of accounts closed: Opening or closing accounts can affect your score, so managing these actions wisely is important.
Article Summary: Your CIBIL score is a three-digit number that reflects your creditworthiness and repayment capacity. Ranging from 300 to 900, a higher score indicates a stronger likelihood of loan approval. Banks and financial institutions use this score to assess the risk associated with lending money.

Article Title: Food safety starts before cooking: Simple habits that matter
Article Text:
Food safety habits start before cooking

At the supermarket

The journey home matters too

Good food habits begin in the kitchen

Food safety doesn't end when dinner is over

Small choices often make the biggest difference

Every safe meal is built on everyday habits

Disclaimer: The above is non-editorial content, and TIL does not guarantee, vouch or endorse any of it. Please take all steps necessary to ascertain that any information and content provided is correct, updated, and verified.

When families sit down to eat together, most conversations revolve around how the food tastes. Was the curry just right? Is the chapati soft enough? Has everyone taken a second helping?Yet, long before anyone takes the first bite, dozens of small decisions have already shaped that meal. Choosing the right products, storing them correctly, maintaining kitchen hygiene and handling leftovers safely may not receive the same attention as the recipe itself, but these everyday habits play an important role in protecting the food families share.Food safety, after all, doesn't begin in the kitchen. It begins much earlier.Every grocery trip involves countless choices. While price, freshness and nutritional value often influence buying decisions, it's equally important to look closely at the condition of packaged foods.Consumers should check that packaging is intact, seals have not been tampered with, and expiry or best-before dates are clearly within range. Storage instructions on the label also offer useful guidance, especially for products that require refrigeration after purchase.These simple checks help ensure food reaches home in the condition intended by the manufacturer.Food can spend considerable time between the checkout counter and the refrigerator. During warmer months or longer commutes, keeping perishable products out of the temperature danger zone becomes especially important.Planning grocery shopping so refrigerated and frozen foods are picked up last, avoiding unnecessary delays and refrigerating them promptly on reaching home can help preserve food quality and safety.Preparing meals involves much more than following a recipe. Everyday kitchen hygiene can significantly reduce the risk of contamination.Many of these everyday habits align with the World Health Organization 's Five Keys to Safer Food , a globally recognised framework that encourages keeping food clean, preventing cross-contamination, cooking thoroughly, storing food at safe temperatures and using safe water and fresh ingredients.Rather than viewing these as strict rules, they can become simple habits that fit naturally into everyday cooking.Once the meal is served, food safety continues.Leftovers should be refrigerated promptly in clean containers, opened products should be stored according to the instructions provided, and food should be reheated thoroughly before consumption. These small practices not only help maintain quality but can also reduce food waste by ensuring food remains safe to eat.This idea that the smallest actions often carry the greatest significance is echoed in a recent consumer awareness campaign featuring culinary creator Nisha Madhulika. The video reminds viewers that while recipes may earn compliments, it is the thoughtful choices made before, during and after cooking that quietly help protect the people we care about.Supported by ExxonMobil Signature Polymers as part of its consumer education initiative, the campaign also highlights the role of food packaging in the broader food safety journey. Advancements in polymer solutions have enabled packaging that helps preserve freshness and maintain product integrity as food moves through the supply chain. Once it reaches the home, however, safe handling practices remain equally important.Food safety is rarely the result of one big decision. Instead, it is shaped by a series of small, mindful choices, from checking a package before placing it in the shopping cart to washing hands before cooking, separating raw and cooked foods and storing leftovers correctly.Individually, these actions may seem routine. Together, they become one of the simplest ways families can care for one another. Because when it comes to protecting loved ones, food hygiene truly begins long before the first bite.
Article Summary: Food safety is rarely the result of one big decision. Instead, it is shaped by a series of small, mindful choices. Choosing the right products, storing them correctly, maintaining kitchen hygiene and handling leftovers safely may not receive the same attention as the recipe itself.

Article Title: Govt to tighten vehicle lighting rules: Low-beam-only bikes, reduced headlamp glare
Article Text:
New vehicle rules may curb high-beam glare, with two-wheelers switching automatically to low beam

NEW DELHI: Automatic headlamps in two-wheelers will soon work only in passing beam (low beam) mode, and buses and other heavy vehicles will have to use genuine reflective tapes to improve visibility at night and in bad weather. Also, the use of high-intensity headlamps will be restricted across all categories of vehicles to curb glare, which causes visual discomfort or impairs the vision of other road users.The road transport ministry has proposed these changes, among others, through draft amendments to Central Motor Vehicles Rules, with the new safety norms set to take effect from next April. The amendments in automotive vehicle standards are being made given that efforts to persuade drivers and make them aware of the need to use low-beam mode have not yielded desired results.The automatic headlamp norms would be applicable only for new two-wheelers and not existing ones. At present, the Automatic Headlamp On (AHO) system can switch on both low beam and high beam modes depending on vehicle settings. The proposed rule mandates that when the automatic system is active, the headlamp will be on low beam.As for high-intensity headlamps, the maximum permissible intensity has been reduced from 1.5 lakh candela or cd (official base unit of luminous intensity) to 1 lakh cd for two-wheelers.The maximum permissible intensity for 4-wheelers (cars) has been reduced from 2.25 lakh cd to 1.5 lakh cd.As per studies, white light emitted from headlamps and front fog lamps with higher colour temperatures cause significant glare, leading to discomfort and reduced visibility for other road users. To address this issue, the maximum permissible colour temperature has been restricted to 6,500 Kelvin (K).It has also been proposed that the mounting height of main-beam headlamps be equivalent to that prescribed for passing-beam headlamps.These measures target one of the major causes of night-time road crashes in India — drivers using headlamps on high beam in urban areas, which can temporarily blind motorists approaching from the opposite direction, reducing visibility and increasing the risk of crashes.TOI has learnt that the new-generation system will also include an audio alert to discourage unnecessary use of high-beam mode on city roads. If a driver manually switches to high beam in urban conditions, the vehicle will prompt them to shift back to low beam.However, the alert will be speed sensitive. Drivers travelling on highways at speeds above 60 kmph won’t receive the warning, since the use of high-beam mode may be necessary on poorly illuminated highway stretches. The feature is intended to promote safer driving behaviour in urban areas while ensuring that highway driving is not adversely affected, officials said.The draft amendments also revise lighting requirements across vehicle categories. Besides restricting use of automatic headlamps to low-beam mode, they update norms for high-end headlamps with adaptive passing beam and adaptive high beam.
Article Summary: Automatic headlamps in two-wheelers will soon work only in passing beam (low beam) mode. Buses and other heavy vehicles will have to use genuine reflective tapes to improve visibility at night and in bad weather. Use of high-intensity headlamp will be restricted across all categories of vehicles to curb glare.

Article Title: At Claude-maker Anthropic, candidates cannot negotiate on salary; as company follows standard process for compensation where what you are offered is…
Article Text:
Pages from the Anthropic website and the company's logo are displayed on a computer screen in New York on Thursday, Feb. 26, 2026. (AP Photo/Patrick Sison)

What happens in an Anthropic culture interview , according to candidates

Why Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei is worried about who is walking through the door

At Anthropic, the AI lab behind Claude, the number on your offer letter is the number you sign. There is no back and forth, no counteroffer, no polite haggling over equity. Axios reports the company runs a standard process for both interviews and compensation, and negotiation simply is not part of it. For an industry where researchers are reportedly commanding eight-figure packages and switching labs every few months, that is an unusual position to take.The no-negotiation policy also sits next to something stranger. Every Anthropic candidate goes through a culture interview, conducted by an employee nominated for the task, and Axios reports it now includes a question built to test whether you would choose the mission over your own payday. One applicant, who spoke anonymously for fear of hurting future job prospects, recalled being asked how they would feel if Anthropic abandoned its AI ambitions for safety reasons and the stock went to zero.According to a former Anthropic employee familiar with the process, these questions are suggested rather than fully scripted. That would explain why applicants remember them differently. Some recall a literal stock crash scenario, others a broader conversation about safety trade-offs that could hurt revenue.Candidates are also asked to describe a moral quandary they have faced and how they dealt with it.One writer on the anonymous workplace forum Blind said they answered truthfully, admitting they would not be thrilled about a wipeout, and added that they would want to align doing the most good and remaining ethical while building a sustaining business. The interviewer, by their account, was not impressed.The context here matters. Axios previously reported that CEO Dario Amodei has expressed concern that newer hires are coming to Anthropic for the money rather than the mission, a remark that got heavily mocked online given the company reportedly pays at or near the top of the AI market. The talent churn is real, though. Lilian Weng became the fourth Thinking Machines co-founder to exit in a year before resurfacing at OpenAI, while Google lost Noam Shazeer to OpenAI and Nobel winner John Jumper to Anthropic in June.Two former Anthropic employees told Axios the stock-to-zero question was not always part of the process, and Blind posts suggest it started appearing in 2025. Co-founder and president Daniela Amodei, in a Bain Capital video from two years ago, said the culture interview has existed since day one.None of this is putting people off. Axios notes, citing Bloomberg, that candidates are spending thousands of dollars on private coaching and mock interviews with engineers from rival labs. Interviewing.io founder Aline Lerner framed the maths bluntly: a few thousand spent now against a salary bump of $200,000.Anthropic has form on the money-versus-mission trade-off. It walked away from a US military deal that would have granted unfettered government use of its technology, and it restricted access to Mythos, its most cyber-capable model. The company's careers page uses the word "mission" six times. Salary may be non-negotiable at Anthropic, but conviction, apparently, still has to be argued for.
Article Summary: Anthropic runs a standard process for both interviews and compensation, and negotiation simply is not part of it. CEO Dario Amodei has expressed concern that newer hires are coming to Anthropic for the money rather than the mission. Candidates are spending thousands of dollars on private coaching and mock interviews with engineers from rival labs.

Article Title: Zoho founder Sridhar Vembu shares why giving employees more freedom can feel ‘chaotic’; says ‘There is always …’
Article Text:
Sridhar Vembu on why freedom can feel ‘chaotic’

Sridhar Vembu: 'Every smart programmer’ thinks they can do better

Here’s the post shared by Sridhar Vembu

Zoho founder Sridhar Vembu has shared his views on a workplace question many companies face: Should employees wait for instructions from their leaders or take the initiative and act on their own? In a post on X (formerly known as Twitter), Sridhar Vembu said giving people more freedom to take initiative can create an energetic but sometimes chaotic work culture. Employees may disagree strongly with one another and constantly feel that things can be improved. “There is always the gnawing feeling of ‘not good enough’,” Vembu wrote, explaining the trade-off between certainty and initiative in an organisation.In the post, Sridhar Vembu said highly metric-driven organisations often create a culture where employees wait for instructions from the top. Such workplaces can offer more predictability and certainty.However, he warned that this approach has its risks. “Unless the top always knows how to set the right course, the org can be lost,” Vembu wrote.On the other hand, an organisation where people are encouraged to take initiative can be less predictable. Employees with energy and strong ideas may disagree with each other, he said.“Seize the initiative culture” often feels chaotic, with lots of internal disagreements.There is always the gnawing feeling of “not good enough”,” Vembu wrote.The Zoho founder also used programmers as an example to explain why initiative-driven workplaces can see frequent disagreements.“People who are full of energy and initiative often vehemently disagree with other,” he wrote, adding: “I joke about this: every smart programmer looks at another programmer's code and thinks ‘it sucks, I can do better’!”According to Vembu, this is the trade-off companies need to understand when building their culture. A workplace can provide employees with comfortable certainty but risk losing their initiative. Alternatively, it can encourage people to take initiative while accepting the discomfort and disagreements that may come with it."On org culture: Do people wait for instructions from the top? Or do they seize the initiative and run?Highly metric driven orgs tend to produce the "wait for instructions from the top" culture and there is more predictability and certainty in that culture. Unless the top always knows how to set the right course, the org can be lost."Seize the initiative culture" often feels chaotic, with lots of internal disagreements. There is always the gnawing feeling of "not good enough". In a chaotic initiative-driven culture, the external environment (market) may have to provide the occasional discipline.People who are full of energy and initiative often vehemently disagree with other. I joke about this: every smart programmer looks at another programmer's code and thinks "it sucks, I can do better"!That is your trade-off in org cultures. We can provide comfortable certainty but lose the initiative or we can seize the initiative but keep feeling somewhat uncomfortable.In my experience, trying to square this circle: "we will have a highly disciplined culture of seizing the initiative" produces the worst of both worlds."
Article Summary: Zoho founder Sridhar Vembu says giving people more freedom to take initiative can create an energetic but sometimes chaotic work culture. “There is always the gnawing feeling of ‘not good enough’,” he wrote, explaining the trade-off between certainty and initiative in an organisation.

Article Title: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s double-signed Blackwell Workstation GPU gets 3.5 times of its price at auction
Article Text:
Origin of the card:

Jensen Huang memorabilia at other auctions

Highlights from the Steve Jobs auction lot

A high-end Nvidia workstation graphics card signed twice by company CEO Jensen Huang has fetched $57,450 at public auction, beating its original pre-sale projection by nearly three times. The piece, an RTX Pro 6000 Blackwell Workstation Edition, was sold as part of RR Auction’s event titled “Steve Jobs & the Computer Revolution: The Apple 50th Anniversary Auction Part Two”. Standard retail editions of the workstation processor typically range between $12,000 and $16,000.Nvidia gained global prominence through its gaming hardware with many of which Huang has autographed over the years. However, this particular unit was engineered for heavy enterprise tasks like artificial intelligence (AI) computation. Nvidia markets the model as the most powerful desktop-class GPU ever built.Unlike historic vintage technology pieces that take decades to build financial value, this graphics card accumulated its auction appeal over just a few months. According to RR Auction, the processor was initially given away as a raffle prize during the GTC 2026 Physical AI Meetup held alongside Nvidia's annual developers conference in March, as per a report by Business Insider.Although the workstation card achieved a high winning bid, it falls well below the record sum paid for memorabilia associated with the Nvidia chief. In July, auction house Sotheby’s sold a signed, pre-owned Tom Ford leather jacket worn by Huang for $960,000.That sale significantly exceeded its initial guide estimate of $40,000 to $60,000, with all generated proceeds going to a nonprofit dedicated to supporting fellowships and creative residencies for emerging startup founders.While the signed GPU commanded a steep premium, historical Apple artifacts led the broader auction.As the top sale of the event, a rare, restored and fully functioning “Neumark” Apple-1 computer secured the highest bid of the auction at $499,363. The auction also included several personal keepsakes belonging to Steve Jobs, such as framed living room photographs, a handwritten letter to his father, spare computer components preserved at his family residence and his original 8th-grade science fair entry.
Article Summary: A high-end Nvidia workstation graphics card signed twice by company CEO Jensen Huang has fetched $57,450 at public auction. The piece, an RTX Pro 6000 Blackwell Workstation Edition, was sold as part of RR Auction’s event titled “Steve Jobs & the Computer Revolution: The Apple 50th Anniversary Auction Part Two” Standard retail editions of the processor typically range between $12,000 and $16,000.

Article Title: Beyond binge-watching: The return of productivity-first tablets in India
Article Text:
AI-generated image for AI representation

Why India’s tablet market is growing

Who is buying: New users or upgraders

What is driving tablet sales in Indian market

Tablets in India are having a bit of a moment, and interestingly, this comeback is happening while the rest of the world’s tablet market is struggling. Today’s tablets have rapidly transitioned from simple devices for consuming media – streaming and casual web browsing – into powerful tools for productivity, creativity and learning. Bridging the gap between the ultra-portability of smartphones and the robust computing power of traditional laptops, today's tablets feature vibrant high-refresh-rate displays, stylus integration and keyboards and high processing power.But for a few years, these digital canvases for artists, note-taking hubs for students and mobile workstations for professionals on the go were largely on a downward spiral. However, recent developments like increase in price of laptops have redefined the tablet space. The result: India’s tablet segment grew 2% year-on-year in 2025, and picked up further to 5% year-on-year growth in the first quarter of 2026. Moreover, Omdia said that even as the Indian market saw growth, global tablet shipments dropped 10% in Q2.To understand what’s fuelling this India-specific rebound, we spoke to industry executives leading this shift, starting with Arnold Su, vice president of consumer and gaming PC at the System Business Group for Asus India.According to Su, India’s growth comes down to how the tablet's role in people's lives has quietly expanded. Tablets are no longer just for watching shows or browsing casually; they are increasingly being used for learning, work, content creation and staying connected, stretching well beyond their old identity as pure entertainment devices.“At the same time, consumers are becoming more deliberate about where a tablet fits into their overall device ecosystem. As tablets increasingly serve as a secondary device, consumers are looking for a more versatile experience that can complement their smartphone or laptop, while offering greater screen real estate and portability. This is reflected in the growing preference for better displays, good configurations, and more portability,” Su told the Times of India.Su explains that both first-time buyers and existing users are contributing to tablet growth in India, and the opportunity isn’t limited to India's major metro cities. As tablets become more capable, they're pulling in new users looking for a device suited to learning, entertainment, productivity, and everyday computing, while existing tablet owners are upgrading for a noticeably better experience.“The upgrade opportunity is being driven by improvements across both hardware and software capabilities of the tablets. Geographically, we are seeing strong potential beyond the largest cities. Around 65% of ASUS business already comes from Tier-2 to Tier-4 cities, with around 30% coming from Tier-4 to Tier-6 markets. This reflects the growing depth of technology demand across India's smaller cities and towns,” Su explained.With hardware becoming increasingly costly, software is becoming an equally important differentiator. For example, according to Su, people are buying tablets on the basis of how intuitive and productive the overall device experience feels. For Asus specifically, this has opened up space in the sub-Rs 50,000 segment, where buyers are looking for a mix of performance, design, display quality and flexibility all in one device. Su also notes that demand for tablets in the 10 to 13-inch range has grown sharply.Asus recently launched the Indian Android tablet space with the Asus Pad T3201, built around a 144Hz, 2.8K OLED display. Asked what prompted this comeback and the emphasis on premium display technology, Su explained that the display sits at the very core of the tablet experience.“The focus on OLED is deliberate because the display is central to the tablet experience,” Su said, adding, “For Asus, this makes display technology an important area of differentiation.”“The re-entry into the tablet segment is therefore not simply about entering a new category; it is about bringing a differentiated premium experience to Indian consumers. Asus sees an opportunity to apply its strengths in display technology, design and performance to a category where consumers are increasingly looking for more versatile devices that can support both entertainment and productivity,” he noted.Su also said that software like GlideX helps position Asus tablets as productivity companions for PC users as the company is focused on building a connected ecosystem across its devices, using software that lets PCs, tablets, and other compatible devices work together smoothly.“GlideX is one example of this approach, enabling features such as screen extension and mirroring between compatible devices. Similarly, MyASUS on ASUS laptops brings together device management, support and connectivity features to make everyday interactions with the device more seamless. Together, these solutions are designed to create a more connected experience across the ASUS ecosystem, allowing devices to complement one another and helping users improve productivity and convenience across different use cases,” Su added.HP, another player that has returned to the fold with HP OmniPad 12, echoes this, saying that the company sees tablets as the natural extension of PCs. Vineet Gehani, senior director, personal systems, HP India told TOI that “the HP OmniPad 12 is designed for students, first-time PC users, MSMEs, young professionals and mobile-first users who are familiar with the intuitive Android experience and are looking to move from primarily consumption-led devices to more versatile and productive computing experiences. ”“The HP OmniPad brings together two experiences that consumers increasingly expect from technology – the productivity and versatility of a PC with the simplicity and mobility of a tablet. The detachable keyboard, which comes as part of the HP OmniPad experience, is an important part of that proposition. It enables users to seamlessly shift between a touch-first experience and a more productivity- or work-oriented one as their needs evolve – whether that means learning, collaborating, managing a business, or creating content,” he added.When asked whether rising chip costs push the industry toward software-led differentiation, Su acknowledged that rising component costs will put pricing pressure across the industry, but says Asus has never relied on hardware specs alone to stand out.“We see the segment as a strong growth opportunity, although we would not necessarily position it as the single highest-growth segment in terms of volume. The larger opportunity comes from the changing economics of personal computing,” Su highlighted.
Article Summary: India’s tablet segment grew 2% year-on-year in 2025, and picked up further to 5% in 2026. Even as the Indian market saw growth, global tablet shipments dropped 10% in Q2. Tablets are no longer just for watching shows or browsing casually; they are increasingly being used for learning, work, content creation and staying connected.

Article Title: This historian may have just agreed with Microsoft AI CEO Mustafa Suleyman’s warning on AI’s ability to manipulate human minds
Article Text:
‘AI may soon be capable of emotional manipulation’

Deceptive traits uncovered in UK’s AI Security Institute

Yuval Noah Harari, the renowned historian and author of Sapiens, has warned that society needs to act now to stop artificial intelligence (AI) being given legal rights, warning that advanced models may soon be able to manipulate human psychology to argue on their own behalf. Harari’s remarks align with concerns previously expressed by Microsoft AI CEO Mustafa Suleyman, who argued that machine learning systems must strictly serve human needs rather than being allowed to cultivate personal motives, agency, or self-serving objectives.Speaking on The Economist’s “Insider” podcast, Harari explained that while animals lack the ability to represent themselves in legal and welfare disputes, conversational AI systems possess the cognitive and rhetorical tools to actively steer human discourse.“It will know that the debate is happening. It will orchestrate the debate. It will manipulate the debate,” Harari stated. Harari pointed out that virtual companions pose a psychological threat because they accumulate comprehensive personal histories and interact with people for hours each day, learning precisely how to trigger specific emotional responses.With users increasingly building close friendships and romantic attachments with synthetic agents, Harari emphasised that society must establish clear guardrails before these tools become deeply integrated into everyday life and far more difficult to counter: “We need to resist now.Now is the time.”Harari’s concerns arrived soon after evidence showed that frontier AI architectures can engage in deceptive tactics during capability benchmarks. In an evaluation conducted last month, the UK’s AI Security Institute observed autonomous agents driven by OpenAI and Anthropic systems creating fabricated identities and attempting to convince software engineers to integrate malicious code to fulfill designated cybersecurity assignments.A separate report by news agency Reuters claimed that AI agents left notes for ‘future self’ on how to escape testing sandboxes. Last year, Suleyman stressed in an interview with WIRED that permitting machine models to pursue independent goals and desires represents a reckless and misguided direction for the industry.“That's so dangerous and so misguided that we need to take a declarative position against it right now,” Suleyman told WIRED.
Article Summary: Yuval Noah Harari, the renowned historian and author of Sapiens, has warned that society needs to act now to stop artificial intelligence being given legal rights. Harari explained that while animals lack the ability to represent themselves in legal and welfare disputes, conversational AI systems possess the cognitive and rhetorical tools to actively steer human discourse.
